title: The official’s own committees as a payer
question: Whom did each official’s campaign and ballot committees pay, and which of those payees later appear as City staff in that official’s office, as an appointee, as a lobbyist contacting that official, or as a City contractor?
finding: The committees of the 36 officials report $77.8 million in itemised payments to 4,408 firms and organizations and 2,157 individuals. 40 official-and-firm pairs are lobbying firms whose lobbyists later reported contacting the same official, 6 are individual registered lobbyists who did, 12 are campaign staff who then started work in the official’s department, 1 shares a rare name with a person the same official later appointed as Mayor, and 69 are firms the City went on to pay.
how: Payments are the expenditure schedule (Schedule E) of every committee the Ethics Commission’s register ties to the official as a candidate, plus ballot-measure committees whose name carries the official’s name; the latest version of each statement is used. Firms are matched by exact name to the lobbyist directory and the City’s payment ledger; City payments are those in fiscal years after the first campaign payment, shown for consultants and for payees paid $5,000 or more; public bodies a committee paid (filing fees, taxes, postage) are left out. Individuals are counted, and named only when registered as a lobbyist who reported contacting the same official, when a Board file records their appointment by the same official as Mayor (rare names only), or when the jobs analysis already lists them as campaign staff who joined the official’s department.
limits: Being connected is not being corrupt. A campaign consultant may also be a registered lobbyist; posts in an elected official’s own office are exempt from civil-service selection (the jobs analysis quotes the rule). A firm the City pays may have won its contracts by open bidding in a department the official never dealt with, and a large company that a campaign paid for advertising or telephone service and that also employs lobbyists is a coincidence of size. Person matches are by name and are labelled; a campaign payee and an appointee of the same rare name are probably, not certainly, one person. Amounts, parties and dates taken from Board file titles are read by machine: in a hand check of 50 titles, 11 had at least one field read wrongly (4 after later fixes).
